---
title: "Preface"
---

This book teaches geospatial artificial intelligence (GeoAI) to readers who come to it from GIS, geography, and urban planning. It is written for a research-centered course that mixes upper-level undergraduates with graduate students, so every chapter is built to work at more than one depth.

## Who this book is for

You do not need a computer science background. You should be comfortable with basic GIS concepts, and some exposure to Python will help, though Part 2 of the course sets up the working environment and reviews the essentials. The book is demanding on purpose. It asks you to think carefully about why a model works, where it will fail, and what that means for the people and places affected by it.

## How each chapter is built

Every chapter follows the same pattern, so you always know where to look.

- **Core** is the main text. It builds the concepts and the code that everyone needs.
- **Try it** boxes give short activities, discussion prompts, and notebooks that put the core ideas to work.
- **Frontier** boxes point to recent research and open problems. They are written for graduate students and anyone who wants to push further, and they are optional for a first read.
- **What could go wrong** boxes describe the ethical issues, biases, and failure modes that belong to the topic at hand. Ethics runs through the whole book and does not get a single chapter of its own.

## Running examples

Four examples return throughout the book, so you can see what each new method changes about a problem you already know.

- California housing prices, which anchors the chapters on tabular data
- Urban heat islands, which bridges tabular data and imagery
- Poverty estimation from satellite imagery, which anchors deep learning and foundation models
- Land cover classification, which anchors image segmentation

## What this book leaves for later

This edition focuses on supervised learning, computer vision, and the evaluation and deployment of models that use them. Methods for text and for graphs are saved for a later volume.
